new_statements.quote: [p. 4] Tone is symbolized by ´ for high tone and low tone is unmarked. [p. 10] All non-verb stems and kwé-V 'continuative' may also be divided into one of two tone classes namely: tone class 1, those morphemes which cause the following morpheme(s) in a close-knit sequence to perturb to low tone and tone class 2, those morphemes which cause the following morpheme(s) in a close-knit sequence to perturb to high tone. A close-knit sequence may be a word which is a non-verb or any Modified Noun Phrase. kwé-V 'continuative' will cause tone perturbation in verbs.
new_statements.citation: Marks, Doreen. 1974. Kosena grammar. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics, ms (155 pp; SIL PNG archive 49802). Sec. 1.1 Orthography, p. 4; sec. 2.1 Morphophonemic Classes, p. 10.
new_statements.locator: p. 4 (p. 6), sec. 1.1 Orthography, last line; p. 10 (p. 12), sec. 2.1, first paragraph
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (162-page scan, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Kosena grammar'), rendered pp. 6 and 12 at 150 dpi and read the page scan directly. Printed p. 4 (p. 6), sec. 1.1 Orthography, last line reads exactly 'Tone is symbolized by ´ for high tone and low tone is unmarked.' after the five-vowel list (i, e, o, u, ʌ; e, o, ʌ lengthenable), twelve consonants and thirteen clusters. Printed p. 10 (p. 12), first paragraph, reads exactly 'All non-verb stems and kwé-V'continuative' may also be divided into one of two tone classes namely: tone class 1, those morphemes which cause the following morpheme(s) in a close-knit sequence to perturb to low tone and tone class 2, those morphemes which cause…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kosena is described as a two-level tone language (high marked with an acute, low unmarked, vowel length also contrastive on e, o, a); every non-verb stem belongs to one of two tone classes that perturb the tones of following morphemes within a close-knit sequence (a non-verb word or a modified noun phrase). No word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the grammar; the word 'stress' never occurs. The reading is therefore 'tonal, no stress statement', not an explicit denial of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: On tone, not stress: 'More investigation is needed in the area of tone perturbation in verbs' (p. 33); reduplicated stems 'Tone pattern is not always predictable' (p. 64); in possessive noun phrases 'tone perturbation does not occur across the word boundaries' (p. 105).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is marked on citation forms of stems and on affixes; tone perturbation operates over the close-knit sequence (non-verb word or Modified Noun Phrase), i.e. word and phrase level. No stress domain is stated. Data are from the Kosena dialect of Auyana (p. 3: 'The data used in this paper is from the Kosena dialect').
new_statements.identity_note: Marks 1974 describes the Kosena dialect of Auyana (Awiyaana). Glottolog 5.1 has retired kose1239 as a bookkeeping entry ('Kosena is a locality where the language in the Auyana entry is spoken', citing McKaughan & Marks 1973: 181) and files Marks 1974, the Kosena-English dictionary and McKaughan & Marks 1973 under awiy1238 (Awiyaana, ISO auy). The catalog's existing awiy1238 record is not determinable and rests on McKaughan & Marks 1973, whose data are also from Kosena village. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this is one entity: the Marks 1974 tone statement should upgrade awiy1238 (tone language, no stress statement) rather than create a second row for kose1239. Usarufa (usar1243, Bee 1965/1973) is a separate key and must not be merged

sources.note: Nothing: the word 'stress' does not occur in the 162 scanned pages (a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|pitch|prominen hits only 'interrogative intonation', p. 3.3 verb section). Sec. 1.1 Orthography (p. 4) gives 5 vowels (e, o, a lengthenable), 12 consonants, 13 clusters, and 'Tone is symbolized by ' for high tone and low tone is unmarked.' Sec. 2.1 (p. 10) sets up two tone classes of non-verb stems that perturb following morphemes in a close-knit sequence (non-verb word or Modified Noun Phrase) to low or high tone; p. 33 'More investigation is needed in the area of tone perturbation…

sources.citation: McKaughan, Howard P. & Doreen Marks. 1973. Notes on Auyana phonology and morphology. In H. McKaughan (ed.), The Languages of the Eastern Family of the East New Guinea Highland Stock, 181-189. Seattle: University of Washington Press. (fn. 1: based on Marks's data papers; p. 181: 'This study is of the dialect spoken by about 350 people living in the village of Kosena')
sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology covers segmental consonants and six vowels only, then sec. 3 Noun Morphophonemics; no sentence on stress, accent or tone (confirmed by a full-text search for stress/accent; catalog record awiy1238 A/B reached the same result). the compilers introduction (ch. X) says Bee's Usarufa chapters 'give the descriptive details for the Auyana language group' and 'highlight (A) tone'.

sources.citation: Marks, Doreen. 1974 [1969-1975]. Kosena to English Dictionary, retyped, completed August 1974. SIL typescript, 358 pp, with handwritten tone marks and grammar notes (Glottolog 'Kosena-English dictionary', 358 pp, filed under awiy1238).
sources.note: No phonology preface; opens with mood/aspect grammar notes then entries. Headwords carry acute tone marks; scattered notes 'N.B. tone', 'tone is incorrect', 'check tone', and one remark '(a being mid tone chose not to write it as high in Mark for disciples)' ( line 2453) implying a phonetic mid level. Nothing on stress.
